asSun.p: Aquarius has two rulers depending on who you ask. The older astrologers gave it Saturn, and the modern ones added Uranus once it was discovered, and you'll probably recognise both in yourself, the part that likes rules and the part that likes breaking them. The Star is Aquarius's card, so with your Sun there it's yours. The awkward bit is that the Sun is in detriment in Aquarius. That means it's in the sign opposite Leo, where the Sun is at home, so its natural wish to be the centre of attention has to work against the grain. You still want to shine. You just want to do it on behalf of something, a group, an idea, a better way of running things, and you get uncomfortable when it's only about you. Aquarius is fixed air, so the ideas stick. Once you've made up your mind about how the world should be, you tend to hold that view for decades.

It comes out as a sort of friendly stubbornness. You'll agree with nearly everyone in a meeting and then quietly do it your own way, and you're mildly surprised when people are cross about that. At a family dinner you're the one who asks why the Christmas arrangements have to be the same every year, and you actually want an answer. Someone at work makes a joke that punches down and you don't laugh, and everyone notices you not laughing. You'd sooner be right about something ten years early than popular about it this year. You also keep odd friendships going for ages, the ex-colleague in Berlin, the neighbour from three houses ago, a group chat that's mostly you sending articles. Being liked matters to you. You're just a bit embarrassed that it does.

The less obvious gift is that you're fair to people you don't much like. Because the Sun is working a bit against the grain in Aquarius, your ego isn't welded to every opinion you hold, and you can hear a good idea from someone who annoys you and say so in front of everyone. I've seen an Aquarius Sun back a junior colleague's proposal over their own in a planning meeting, without any fuss, because it was simply better. People remember that for years. You're also good with strangers in trouble. The woman whose car's broken down, the lost kid at the footy, the new person at the club standing on their own, you're over there before most people have registered it. You don't need to know them first. Fixed air gives you a loyalty to people in general that doesn't wait for a friendship to form.

You can care about people in general so well that the particular ones miss out. You'll spend a Saturday at a working bee for the community garden and forget to ring your mum back about her test results. There's also a contrary streak that's tied up with who you think you are. If everyone likes a thing, you're already a bit suspicious of it, and if a friend agrees with you too quickly you'll sometimes shift your position just to keep a little distance. That's the detriment again. The Sun in Aquarius can feel that being ordinary is a kind of disappearing, so you guard your differences, and it gets lonely after a while. And when someone tells you you've hurt them, you go straight to explaining your reasoning, which is the one thing they didn't ask for.

When things go wrong, your first move is to get organised and a bit remote. A redundancy, a breakup, a bad diagnosis in the family, and by the evening you're on the laptop making a spreadsheet of options, sounding calm on the phone. People take the calm at face value. A week later you're still calm on the outside, you've stopped answering anyone who wants to talk about feelings, and you may have thrown yourself into somebody else's crisis because that one's easier to fix. Fixed air holds a position, and under strain the position is usually 'I'm fine, I've thought it through'. The people close to you feel shut out. You'll discuss the problem with them for hours and still not say you're scared. What helps is a friend who'll sit with you without solving anything, and something to do with your hands, the garden, a long walk, a bike that needs fixing.

You want a partner who's also a friend, and most days you'd take that over the fireworks. Leo is your opposite sign, and a lot of Aquarius Suns end up with someone who has some Leo in them, warm, a bit showy, wanting to be adored in public. That irritates you and it's also exactly what you need to learn from, because they're comfortable being the centre of someone's world and you often aren't. You need room. Separate friends, a night a week that's yours, a partner who doesn't read your independence as a threat. The thing to watch is that you can be so busy being reasonable that you forget to be romantic. Say the soppy thing now and then. Book the dinner. Your partner knows you respect them, and they'd still like to hear that you'd pick them.

Work has to be for something. You can put up with a dull job for a while if you believe in what the organisation's doing, and you'll be miserable in a well-paid one you think is pointless. The Sun's detriment shows up at work as an uneasy relationship with credit. You want your ideas to win, but you don't want to be seen chasing a promotion, so you undersell yourself at review time and then feel quietly hard done by. You're good at systems, at spotting that the whole team is doing something the long way round, and at getting a room of very different people to pull together on one project. You're less good at hierarchy. A manager who says 'because I said so' will lose you inside a month. Aim for places flat enough that a good idea can come from anywhere.

At twenty an Aquarius Sun is often the rebel with a cause, or several causes, and a strong opinion about how everyone else is living. You can be quite hard on people who don't think the way you do, and you're lonelier than you let on. The Sun working against the grain feels sharpest at that age, when you want to be seen and would hate to be seen wanting it. By the mid-thirties most have found their people, a group, a movement, a workplace, a band of friends, and the edges soften because you don't have to prove you're different any more. You get more practical about change too. The fifties tend to be good years. The Saturn side of the sign comes forward, you become the one who actually knows how the committee works, and younger people bring you their unlikely plans because you won't laugh at them.

Once this week, when someone asks what you think, give your own preference before your principle. 'I'd like Thai' before 'well, it depends what everyone wants'. 'I missed you' before 'it makes sense to catch up'. It'll feel oddly exposing, and that feeling is the Sun in detriment talking. Do it three times over the week and notice who looks pleased.

asMoon.p: The Moon has no special dignity in Aquarius. It's a visitor there, neither helped nor held back, so it takes a lot of its colour from the sign's ruler, which is Saturn in the old system and Uranus in the modern one. Saturn gives your feelings some reserve and some discipline, and Uranus makes them arrive in sudden shifts. The Star belongs to Aquarius, and with your Moon there it becomes the card of how you feel and what you need in order to feel safe. Have a look at the figure on the card, kneeling out in the open at night with nothing around her. That's a fair picture of how you recover. You need air and distance and a bit of sky. Aquarius is a fixed sign as well, which means that once a feeling has properly settled in you, it takes a long while to change its mind.

You tend to think a feeling before you feel it. Someone says something unkind at a barbecue and you're halfway through working out why they said it before you notice you're hurt. A friend cries on the phone and you're good with them, really good, and then you hang up and need an hour of quiet with nobody talking. A Sunday with nothing planned is often bliss for you, a long walk and a podcast and no obligations, where other people would feel lonely. You need your own room, or at least your own corner, and your own time to go to bed. Too much closeness at once, a week of houseguests, a partner who wants to talk through every mood, and you start to feel oddly airless. Then something small happens, a kind message from someone you barely know, and you're moved out of all proportion.

Other people's moods don't flood you. When your housemate's in a foul temper or your teenager slams a door, you can notice it, leave it with them, and get on with dinner, and that's rarer than you'd think. It means people can be difficult around you without being punished for it. You're also a good friend to people who are a bit odd or out of step, because you never needed anyone to be normal to feel comfortable with them. I've seen an Aquarius Moon be the one person a very shy colleague would eat lunch with, every day for a year. And you keep up with people over long gaps. Three years without speaking and you pick up where you left off, with no guilt on either side.

Your need for space can look like not needing anyone at all, and after a while you start believing that yourself. You ask for help later than you should, usually after the thing's already sorted. A partner asks what's wrong and you say you're just tired, and you mean it, because you genuinely haven't looked yet. The Saturn colouring can make you strict with your own feelings, as if some of them are allowed and some are a bit embarrassing. Jealousy, neediness, missing someone, those go in a drawer. And because Aquarius is fixed, an old hurt can harden into a principle. You stop going to the family Christmas and say it's about the politics, when really it's about one thing your dad said in 2014.

Your first move under stress is to withdraw into logic. Grief, a job loss, a friend's betrayal, and you go into your head and start reading everything you can find on the subject, or reorganising the spare room at midnight. You'll tell people what happened in a very level voice. A week later the feeling usually comes through, often somewhere strange, in a film, at a stranger's kindness in a shop, and it can knock you flat for an afternoon. With Uranus colouring this Moon, the waves tend to come suddenly. The people around you can feel locked out during that first week, and they sometimes back off, thinking you want them to, which leaves you alone longer than is good for you. What helps is company that doesn't ask questions. Someone on the other end of the couch, a walk beside a friend, a meal cooked for you.

In love you need to be able to breathe. That sounds cold on paper, and in practice it's simple. You love someone better when you're allowed to miss them. A partner who texts all day or wants every evening together can leave you feeling hemmed in, however much you care about them. Friendship sits underneath everything for you, and the relationships that last are the ones where you actually like each other on an ordinary Tuesday. You show affection in slightly unusual ways. You'll remember the exact tea they like, fix their bike, send them an article at two in the morning because it made you think of them. Tell them that's what it is. They may not work it out on their own, and a partner with a warmer, louder Moon can read your quiet as a lack of love.

You need a bit of autonomy to feel safe at work. Being micromanaged gets under your skin physically, and an open-plan office with no quiet corner tires you in a way you can't quite put into words. Working from home often suits you far better than it suits your colleagues. You're steady with upset clients and colleagues, because you don't catch their panic, and that makes you good to have around in a crisis or in any job that deals with people on their worst days. The catch is that you can seem unbothered when you're actually rattled, so managers underestimate what a restructure or a clash with someone has cost you. Tell them. Notice too that you do your best work when you feel part of a team you believe in, even if you mostly keep to yourself inside it.

At twenty an Aquarius Moon often feels like the odd one out, in the family especially, and has learnt to keep feelings at arm's length because that was the safe option at home. Friends matter enormously, and a group of them can become the family you actually rely on. Through the thirties there's usually a reckoning with closeness. A relationship or a child asks you to be available in a way that doesn't come naturally, and you find, sometimes to your surprise, that you can do it on your own terms. The Saturn side helps here, because it gives you staying power. By the fifties most have a settled, unfussy emotional life, a few deep friendships, plenty of warm acquaintances, and a calm that other people find restful. The risk later on is getting a bit set in your solitude.

Next time you catch yourself explaining a feeling instead of having it, stop and name it in one word, out loud or on paper. Hurt. Lonely. Jealous. Relieved. Don't add the reason, just the word. Then, if someone's with you, tell them the word and let them respond before you add any context. It's uncomfortable the first few times, and it does get easier.

asRising.p: Your rising sign is the one that was coming up over the eastern horizon when you were born. It sets up the first house, which is your body, your manner and the way you go into things. With Aquarius rising, Saturn becomes your chart ruler (Uranus as well, if you use the modern rulers), and The Star, as Aquarius's card, is the one people meet first. Saturn at the front of a chart gives a certain reserve, a slightly formal or self-contained way of holding yourself, and Uranus adds a flash of something unexpected. Most people with this rising have both, and you can see them switch. The fixed air part means your manner is consistent. You're pretty much the same with the barista as you are with the CEO, and people notice that about you, sometimes before they've noticed anything else.

People often say they couldn't read you at first. At a new job you're friendly to everyone in the first week and nobody can tell who you actually like. At a party you'll talk to the person no one else is talking to, have a long, odd conversation about train timetables or fungi, and leave without saying goodbye. Your style is usually a bit off to one side. It might be one strange piece of jewellery with an otherwise plain outfit, or the same black jumper every day for years. When you walk into a room you look around it before you commit to a corner. Strangers tell you surprising things on buses and in queues, because you look like you won't judge them. And you start projects in a sudden burst, then go quiet while you work out the structure.

You put people on an equal footing without meaning to. Your manner doesn't change with status, so the cleaner and the chair of the board both get the same interested, slightly detached attention, and both of them tend to like you for it. That makes you good in rooms where there's a power imbalance, a parent-teacher interview, a job interview with a nervous candidate, someone's first day. The other gift is that your instincts about where things are heading are often early. You'll say a café won't last, or a colleague's about to leave, or a friend's relationship has run its course, and a few months on it turns out you had it. You don't always know why you knew. That's the Uranus side of Aquarius, the sudden read of a situation.

The reserve that makes you easy to trust can also make you hard to reach. People take the cool first impression as the whole story, and you let them, because correcting it would mean showing more than you'd like. At work drinks you'll be pleasant to everyone for two hours and come home having told no one a single real thing. Saturn ruling the chart can put a guardedness into the body itself, the folded arms, the slightly stiff way of sitting, and people read that as judgement when it's actually nerves. There's also a habit of reacting against whatever's expected of you in the moment. Someone tells you to calm down and you get sharper. Someone assumes you'll go along with the plan and suddenly you've got objections you didn't have five minutes ago.

Under pressure your manner gets flatter and more controlled. A car accident, a hard phone call from the hospital, a public row at work, and you're the one who goes very still and starts giving practical instructions. Saturn, your chart ruler, is good at that. People around you feel steadied and a little unnerved at once, because you've shown no feeling at all. A week or so later the body tends to collect. Stiff neck, bad sleep, restless legs, or a sudden urge to change something big, quit the job, cut your hair off, move house. That's Uranus wanting out. Friends can be startled by the swing from calm to drastic, and a bit hurt that they didn't see it coming. What helps is exercise that's properly tiring, and one person you'll admit to that you've been shaken.

With Aquarius rising, Leo falls on your seventh house, the house of partners. So the people you're drawn to are often warmer and louder than you, happy to take the spotlight, generous in a way that seems a bit much at first. They teach you something about simply enjoying being adored, which doesn't come easily to someone with your reserve. The early stages can be tricky. You come across as friendly and detached, and a potential partner often can't tell whether you're interested, so tell them. Taurus sits on your fourth house, home, which means that behind the front door you want things stable, comfortable and a bit old-fashioned, good food, a proper bed, routines that don't change. That surprises people who fell for the unconventional first impression, usually in a good way.

Scorpio is on your tenth house, career and public standing, so however breezy you look, your working life tends to be intense and fairly private. You're often drawn to work that goes deep, research, investigation, therapy, finance, anything where you get to find out what's really going on. The first impression helps. In interviews you come across as calm and a bit original, and people remember you afterwards. Colleagues see someone easygoing, and then they watch you refuse to budge on something you think matters, and it throws them. You tend to do well once people know you. The risk is that your reserve reads as a lack of ambition, so the promotion goes to someone louder. Say what you want, out loud, to the person who decides.

At twenty Aquarius rising often looks older and cooler than it feels. You might have been the kid who dressed strangely, or the one everyone thought didn't care, and a lot of that was shyness in disguise. Through the thirties the Saturn side starts to pay off. You get a reputation for being reliable and fair, the manner turns into a kind of calm authority, and people start asking you to chair things. The unexpected streak doesn't go away, and it often shows up as one big change somewhere in that decade that no one saw coming. By the fifties the look usually settles into something distinctive and unmistakably yours, and the reserve eases. Younger people find you easy to talk to, which would have surprised you at twenty.

At the next gathering where you know hardly anyone, tell the first person you speak to one true thing about yourself inside five minutes. Something small, like the fact that you nearly didn't come, or that you've had a strange week. Watch what it does to the conversation. Your reserve does a useful job most of the time, and this is only a test of what happens when you open the door a crack.

asBirthCard.p: This card comes from your birthdate, and it has nothing to do with where your Sun or Moon happen to sit. Add up every digit of the date, and if the total goes over 22, add its digits again. You landed on 17, which is The Star. Seventeen is built from one and seven, a beginning and the number of searching, and those two add up to eight, the number of Strength, so there's a toughness folded inside this gentle-looking card. Then look at where it sits. Card 16 is The Tower, the lightning strike and the collapse. Card 18 is The Moon, the confusing night where nothing is clear. The Star is the quiet stretch in between. The card's own astrology is Aquarius, fixed air, ruled by Saturn and in modern astrology by Uranus as well, and that's where the card gets its long view and its oddly steady hope.

As a pattern across a life, 17 tends to show up as a run of rebuilding. Something falls down, your parents split when you're a kid, a business goes under, a move to a new city goes badly, and you find yourself in the aftermath doing the quiet work of starting again. You might notice you've been the one who organised the meal roster when a friend's partner died, or the one who kept the group chat going after the big falling-out. At work you're the person people come to after the restructure, when everyone else is sulking. Your own hard times seem to come in the same shape. A shock, a bad few months, then a slow and slightly surprising recovery that leaves you better off than before. After a few rounds of it you start to trust the pattern, a bit.

The quieter gift is that you're hard to shame about your own low points. Because you've come back from things before, you can talk about the divorce or the breakdown or the year you were broke without much embarrassment, and that gives other people permission to talk about theirs. I've watched someone with this birth card mention, over a work lunch, that they'd once been sacked, and within ten minutes the whole table was swapping stories they'd never told. There's also a patience with slow things, a garden, a friendship that's taking years to thaw, a skill you're rubbish at, and you don't need a result to keep turning up. That's the eight hidden inside the seventeen.

You can get comfortable in the aftermath. If you've spent a lot of your life rebuilding, calm can start to feel suspicious, and some people with this card quietly go looking for the next thing to fix. A friend in crisis, a partner who needs rescuing, a failing project at work you volunteer for when your plate's already full. You can also hand out hope to others that you won't give yourself. You'll tell a mate their redundancy is the start of something, and in the same week call your own setback proof that you always mess things up. The Tower and The Moon sit either side of this card, and living between them can leave you braced for the next storm when nothing's actually coming.

When the bottom falls out, the first thing you do is get practical and a little too cheerful. You make lists, ring around, reassure everyone, including the people who should be reassuring you. A week later the next card in the sequence often turns up, the foggy, anxious Moon stretch where you can't sleep and everything looks worse at 3 a.m. You don't tell many people about that part, because you're known as the hopeful one and it feels wrong to fall apart. So the people around you get a slightly brittle version of you and can't work out why. What actually helps is rest first and plans later. Sleep, food, a day off, and one person who knows you well enough to say you don't have to be the optimist this time.

In love you're drawn to honesty over polish. You'd take someone who'll admit they're scared over someone who's always charming, and you tend to be very open early on, which some partners find disarming and others find a bit much. A lot of people with this card meet their important partners during or just after a hard stretch, and the relationship carries some of that feeling of recovery in it. That can be lovely. It can also mean you stay in the role of healer long after the other person's healed. Keep checking that the relationship still has room for you to be the one who's struggling. And let yourself be pleased when it's going well. Some of you wait for the other shoe to drop, and a partner can feel that.

The pattern suits work where things get put back together. Nursing, rehab, counselling, rescuing a failing shop, turnaround work in a company, teaching kids who've had a rough start, restoring old furniture, disaster recovery. You're steadiest in the part of the job everyone else finds depressing, the long middle where nothing looks better yet. The Aquarian streak in the card itself shows up as an interest in fairness and in how things could be organised better, so you may end up on the committee or pushing for a change to the roster. The danger is becoming the team's permanent morale officer. When the office leans on you to keep spirits up, it's fine to say you're tired, and fine to let someone else bring the cake.

In the twenties this card often shows up as a first real collapse and a first real recovery, a degree abandoned, a big relationship ending, a move that doesn't work, and the discovery that you come back. It's also when a lot of people with 17 are at their most idealistic and most easily let down. By the mid-thirties most have been through the cycle two or three times and stopped being surprised by it. The hope gets sturdier and less naive, and you start to be the one others seek out after their own Tower moment. The fifties usually bring a more settled version. Fewer storms, or maybe you just see them coming earlier, and a strong wish to pass on what you've learnt, to kids, to a younger colleague, to anyone starting over.

Keep a short list somewhere private of the times you came back from something. The job you lost and the one that followed. The breakup and who you became afterwards. The illness, the move, the year that went wrong. Just a line each. When the next bad stretch arrives, read it before you decide what the setback says about you. Add to it as the years go on.
